correctness.rationale: Direct multiplication gives ad, df and ae+bf as the only possibly nonzero square coordinates. The annihilator line kE14 must be in every maximal admissible space. If d is not identically zero, the products of linear functionals ad=df=0 force a=f=0, including over F₂: independent functionals can both be made one, and proportional nonzero ones cannot have identically zero product. In the slice d=0, quotient by kE14 turns the remaining quadratic into det M=0. Normalize one nonzero rank-one member to E11; applying the determinant to B and B+E11 forces B22=0, then B12 B21=0, so the common-image or common-row classification holds over any field. Each such space extends to a ruling plane, and exactly the row with first coordinate zero extends further by adding a middle-coordinate direction in W₀. Products in the slice are central, so all lifts are associative subalgebras. On the column ruling the product coefficient is p₁p₂ times the alternating determinant of the two row parameters; fixed-row spaces and W₀ have zero products. This gives q−1 nonzero-product algebras including in characteristic two, when the table is commutative. The ruling intersections and replacement of the exceptional row give K_(q+1,q+1). Each nonzero rank-one quotient point selects exactly one space from each ruling; adding W₀ and the annihilator incidence gives the three stated strata and total 2q⁴−q².
residual_risks: The original enumeration over F₂ and F₃ tests subspaces of dimensions three through six; excluding smaller maximal spaces over all fields rests on the plane extension argument. The independent check adds F₄ but is also finite.

evidence: Classical two-ruling geometry gives the linear planes in the determinantal slice. The pair record also gives the one-point equations used to decompose the locus. The exceptional row can be recognized by its intersection with the upper-right block.

A pair in an admissible space satisfies XY+YX=0, not necessarily XY=YX in odd characteristic. The determinant ruling alone therefore does not say which maximal spaces are algebras with nonzero multiplication.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Substantial geometric ingredients and routine consequences are covered; the residual embedded result requires the exceptional replacement, the oriented row/column multiplication computation and its field-dependent consequences. The point-incidence graph and multiplicities then follow from that classification.

evidence: Modulo the common annihilator, the d=0 slice is a split 2×2 determinant cone, so its maximal linear pieces are the classical two rulings. Maximal inclusion in the entire locus differs from maximal inclusion in that slice and also from maximal dimension.

The preserver paper concerns maps preserving the square-zero locus; the full text could not be inspected. The Borel-orbit sources concern orbit closures of individual matrices, not subspace inclusion.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Neither preservers nor Borel point orbits are an equivalent classification of embedded admissible k-linear subspaces with products. The rank-one classification covers the slice component of the argument.

value.rationale: This small fixed-flag algebra exhibits both an exceptional maximal dimension and a nontrivial distinction between the two otherwise symmetric rulings at the level of multiplication. The subspace incidence answers how often a square-zero element extends to a maximal admissible algebra; the product census shows when that extension can have nonzero products despite every element squaring to zero. The characteristic-two result and all-prime-power uniformity make it a useful exact baseline, beyond classifying the two algebraic components of a point locus.
residual_risks: No classification up to conjugacy, scheme structure, or theorem for larger matrix sizes is claimed.
